# Channel Conflict, and How to Manage It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Channel conflict happens when two routes to the same customer compete for the same deal: a direct seller and a reseller, two partners, or a marketplace listing and a partner quote. It cannot be removed, because most B2B technology still reaches buyers through partners and the direct team will always meet them in the same accounts. It can be kept small. The evidence suggests that how often conflict happens matters more than how bad any one dispute gets, so the aim is fewer disputes, settled fast, under rules written down before the first one arrives. Every ruling should be recorded with its reason, because the rulings are what improve the rules.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Canalys estimated that partners would deliver about 70% of global IT spending in 2025, so most technology sellers run more than one route to market.
- Academic work on hybrid channels found that conflict frequency hurts channel performance while conflict intensity does not, which makes prevention more valuable than arbitration.
- In a CompTIA survey of 350 IT channel firms, more than three-quarters had lost at least one deal to channel conflict in a year, and 30% had dropped a vendor over it.
- Rules of engagement need to settle five questions in advance: who registered first, who owns the account, how the direct team is paid on partner deals, which prices are floors and how fast a dispute is ruled on.
- Competition law limits what a supplier can tell or require of its resellers, particularly on pricing and online sales, and in the EU the 2022 vertical rules set the frame.

Part 14 of this series covered how to design a partner channel and Part 18 covered co-selling with the large platforms. Both end in the same place. Once a firm sells through more than one route, two of its routes will eventually want the same customer. A partner registers an opportunity the direct team has been working for a month. A reseller discovers the vendor quoted the same buyer a lower price. A marketplace listing undercuts a partner who did the discovery work.

None of this is a failure of goodwill. It is what happens when the rules are unwritten, the incentives point in different directions and nobody has the authority to rule quickly. This piece covers where the conflict comes from, what the evidence says it costs and the small set of rules that keep it contained.

## Where channel conflict comes from

Channel conflict takes three common forms. Each has a different trigger and needs a different first rule.

| Type | Typical trigger | Who usually loses | First rule to write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical: vendor direct team against a partner | Both work the same account; the direct team is paid only on direct deals | The partner, then the vendor's reputation in the channel | Account ownership and compensation on partner-sourced deals |
| Horizontal: partner against partner | Two partners register the same opportunity, or one discounts into another's territory | The partner with the weaker relationship to the vendor | Deal registration: first valid registration wins, with a stated expiry |
| Multichannel: marketplace or online against partner | The customer finds a lower price on a listing or website than in the partner's quote | The partner who did the pre-sale work | Price floors per route, and a rule for crediting partner influence |

The underlying cause in all three is the same: two parties each believe they have a claim, and there is no prior agreement about whose claim wins. Most firms write the partner agreement carefully and leave the operating rules to custom. Custom works while volumes are low. It stops working when the second or third dispute in a quarter is settled differently from the first.

## What the evidence says it costs

The scale of partner routes is the starting point. Canalys estimated that partner-delivered IT would account for about 70% of global IT spending in 2025, down slightly from 73% in 2023 as some buying moved to direct and marketplace routes. Omdia reported in February 2026 that partners would capture 79% of small and mid-size business IT spending in 2026, with the share above 80% in EMEA and Latin America. A technology firm selling to mid-size buyers is very unlikely to reach most of them without a partner somewhere in the chain.

The cost of conflict is less well measured, and the best survey data is old. CompTIA's 2013 study of 350 US IT channel executives found that 60% said conflict with vendors had risen over two years, more than three-quarters had lost at least one deal to it in the previous year, and 30% had dropped a vendor as a partner. More than 80% said a deal registration programme was critical or important when choosing a vendor. The figures are more than a decade old, but the mechanics they describe have not changed, and no more recent independent survey of the same scope is available.

The most useful finding for practice comes from academic work. Webb and Hogan's study of hybrid channels, published in the *Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing*, found that conflict was a significant determinant of both channel performance and satisfaction. Conflict frequency had a negative effect on channel performance; conflict intensity did not. A partner can absorb one serious dispute that is settled fairly. What wears a channel down is the steady drip of small disputes, each settled by whoever argues hardest.

There is also an opportunity cost. The Ebsta and Pavilion 2024 benchmark, a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, reported that partnership channels returned 3.8 times the sales velocity of other channels, yet only 8% of the businesses in the sample had one. Firms that avoid partners to avoid conflict give that up.

> A channel can survive one hard dispute settled fairly. It does not survive twenty small ones settled by whoever shouted loudest.

## The rules that keep conflict small

The mechanism is simple to describe. Write the rules before the dispute, make the most common rulings automatic, and give one named person the authority to rule on the rest within a stated time. The five questions below cover most disputes in a mid-size firm.

| Rule | What it settles | What to record each time it is used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deal registration | Which partner has the claim on a new opportunity, for how long, and what counts as a valid registration | Registration date, partner, expiry, whether it was accepted and why |
| Account ownership | Which accounts the direct team keeps, which belong to partners, and how an account changes hands | Owner, reason for any change, who approved it |
| Compensation on partner deals | Whether direct sellers are paid when a partner closes in their territory, so they have no reason to compete | The rule applied, and any exception granted |
| Price floors by route | The lowest price each route may offer, so the marketplace, website and partner quotes do not undercut each other by accident | Any quote below the floor, who approved it, the reason |
| Dispute ruling | Who rules, within how many working days, and how a ruling is appealed | The dispute, the ruling, the reason, the owner and the expected effect |

Deal registration does most of the work. The CompTIA survey found that partners' complaints about registration programmes were mainly about poor communication (61%), technical difficulties (49%) and inconsistent rules (27%). Each is fixable without new software: one published rule set, one form, and an answer within a stated number of days.

Compensation is the rule firms most often leave out, and it decides whether the others hold. If a direct seller earns nothing when a partner closes an account in their territory, the seller has every reason to compete for it. Many firms pay the direct team a share, or the full rate, on partner deals in their patch. That costs margin, and it is usually cheaper than the conflict it prevents.

The dispute rule matters because speed is part of fairness. A ruling that takes three weeks has already decided the deal, because the customer has moved on.

## What the law allows

Some conflict-management tools cross into competition law, and a firm should take advice before using them. In the EU, Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/720, the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation, entered into force on 1 June 2022 and replaced the 2010 rules. Its accompanying Vertical Guidelines govern much of what a supplier may agree with its distributors.

Three points matter for channel conflict. First, dual distribution, where a supplier sells directly while also selling through resellers, remains covered, and the exemption now extends to importers and wholesalers as well as manufacturers. Information exchanged between supplier and reseller in that setting is exempt only where it is directly related to implementing the agreement or needed to improve production or distribution. A supplier that asks partners for their pipeline and margin data to settle disputes needs to stay inside that line. Second, under the Guidelines, dual pricing (charging a reseller different prices for online and offline sales) is no longer treated as a hardcore restriction and is assessed case by case. Third, restrictions on selling through online marketplaces can benefit from the exemption if the reseller can still sell through its own website, but a complete ban on price comparison sites or search advertising would not.

The practical point is narrow. Price floors and route rules are legitimate tools inside a firm's own pricing. Telling independent resellers what price they must charge is a different matter in most jurisdictions. Write the rules for what the firm controls, and take advice on anything that binds a partner's own pricing.

## Treat every ruling as a decision

The final step is the one that makes the rules improve. Each dispute ruling is a commercial decision with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected effect, which is the shape of the decision record set out in Part 9 of The Build Order. Recorded that way, a quarter of rulings shows patterns that no single dispute reveals.

Three measures are worth tracking monthly. The number of disputes per hundred registered opportunities tells you whether the rules are preventing conflict; the Webb and Hogan finding says this is the number that matters most. The median days to a ruling tells you whether the process is fast enough to be fair. The share of rulings appealed, or reversed on appeal, tells you whether the rules are clear. A rising appeal rate usually means a rule is ambiguous, and the fix is to rewrite the rule, not to rule harder.

Illustrative example: a registration dispute settled once

Decision
:   A partner's registration on a mid-size account was upheld against the direct team, which had been in early conversations without logging them.

Reason and owner
:   The partner's registration was valid, complete and inside its 90-day window; the direct team's activity was not in the CRM. Ruled by the head of partnerships within three working days.

What changed
:   The direct seller was paid the agreed overlay on the partner deal, and the rules were amended so that direct activity counts against a registration only if it is logged before the registration date.

Illustrative: a composite of a software firm selling through regional resellers, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Prevent rather than arbitrate.** Conflict frequency damages a channel more than conflict intensity, so rules that stop disputes are worth more than a good referee.
- **Pay the direct team on partner deals.** Without it, the other rules will be tested every week.
- **Rule fast and in writing.** A slow ruling decides the deal by default.
- **Record each ruling with its reason.** The pattern across rulings is what tells you which rule to rewrite.

Gateway card

### Before you add a second route to market

- Deal registration rules published, with a validity window and a stated response time
- Account ownership list agreed between direct and partner leads
- Direct-team compensation on partner deals decided and written into the plan
- Price floors set for each route the firm controls
- One named person with authority to rule on disputes, and a deadline for rulings
- Legal advice taken on any rule that touches partner pricing or online sales

## Common questions

### What is channel conflict in B2B sales?

Channel conflict is competition between two routes to the same customer, such as a vendor's direct team and a reseller, two partners, or a marketplace listing and a partner quote, for the same deal.

### How does deal registration reduce channel conflict?

Deal registration gives the first partner to register a valid opportunity a protected claim for a set period, so the vendor and other partners know whose deal it is before they compete.

### Should direct salespeople be paid on partner deals?

Many firms pay the direct team some or all of their usual rate on partner deals in their territory, because a seller who earns nothing from a partner deal has an incentive to compete for it.

### Can a supplier set the prices its resellers charge?

In most jurisdictions a supplier cannot fix the resale price an independent reseller charges. In the EU, Regulation 2022/720 and its Guidelines set the rules for distribution agreements, and firms should take legal advice before restricting partner pricing or online sales.
